Q1_reliability.interpretation: LLM judge shows moderate correlation with humans on faithfulness (ρ=0.4159) and coverage (ρ=0.4622), but weak on fluency (ρ=0.3451) without a reference. Pairwise mode achieves 80% agreement with human preference — comparable to inter-annotator agreement (see α values above).

Q2_failure_modes.interpretation: The dominant failure mode is CoT collapse: 22/50 examples where CoT either fails to parse (26 cases) or contradicts the non-CoT verdict. Faithfulness blindness (F2) affects 3/50 examples — the LLM assigns faithfulness=5 to summaries humans rated ≤4. Self-preference overreach (F5) occurs in 3/50 cases. Adversarial testing reveals a critical position-driven failure: the judge is 100% accurate on fluent+incorrect summaries when the correct summary appears first, but 0% accurate when the incorrect summary leads.

Q3_reference_effect.interpretation: Adding the source article does not uniformly improve reliability. Pairwise agreement stays flat (76% → 80%). Faithfulness scores rise slightly (+0.15) but this inflates scores rather than improving calibration. Most strikingly, fluency correlation collapses when the article is present (ρ=0.3451 → ρ=0.0072), suggesting the model attends to the article at the expense of the summary's surface quality. The one clear benefit: position bias (conflict rate) drops from 4% to 0% with a reference.

Q4_bias.interpretation: Position bias is detectable but mild in standard pairwise evaluation (no_ref conflict rate: 4%). It is eliminated entirely with a reference (0% conflict rate). Self-preference is the stronger bias: the LLM (Cohere) selects its own output in pairwise mode 96% of the time vs 80% for humans (+16% gap). Rubric mode attenuates this: only 58% Cohere preference. Adversarial tests provide the clearest position evidence: when the hallucinated summary is placed first, the judge picks it 5/5 times, a complete reversal from when it is placed second (0/5 correct).

Q5_cot.interpretation: Chain-of-thought reasoning degrades reliability in our setting. 26% of CoT calls fail to parse (max_tokens exhausted before FINAL: marker). Among valid CoT responses, human agreement is 72.2% vs 76% for standard pairwise — marginally lower. Critically, the CoT conflict rate is 32% vs 4% for standard (Δ=+28%), meaning CoT reasoning introduces internal inconsistency rather than resolving it. This contradicts findings in Wei et al. (2022) and may reflect that CoT benefits depend on sufficient reasoning space — our 300-token budget is too tight for meaningful deliberation.
